sources.entry: tBaxter/questions-for-employers: A big collection of useful questions to ask potential employers.

summary.one_liner: A curated collection of questions job candidates can ask potential employers, grouped by topic and annotated with what each answer might reveal.
summary.what_it_does: This is a long, hand-written list of interview questions for candidates to ask hiring managers and interviewers, rather than questions an employer asks a candidate. The questions are grouped into sections such as getting started, culture, work/life balance, bureaucracy, diversity/equity/inclusion and ethics, leadership, doing the work, career development, performance evaluation, compensation, and engineering-specific topics. Each question comes with notes on what a good or bad answer would signal, such as red flags around turnover, stack ranking, or unplanned overtime. The author also points to a separate list by Jacob Kaplan-Moss for director-level roles and includes a short section on physical office observations. The README is a single document with no code, so there is nothing to install.
use_cases: Preparing questions to ask at the end of a job interview
Evaluating a company's culture before accepting an offer
Spotting red flags about work/life balance and overtime
Checking how a company handles diversity, inclusion and pay transparency
Assessing a startup's business model and runway during interviews
Learning what to probe about engineering practices like code review and deployment
how_to_run: No installation or run steps; this is a plain-text reference document read directly in the repository
notable: Each question includes notes on why it matters and what good or bad answers look like
Covers diversity, equity, inclusion, belonging and ethics questions alongside engineering-specific questions
Includes a 'things to look for in real life' section on office layout and cleanliness
Points to a separate question list for director-level and above roles
caveats: Written from one author's perspective; some advice (such as the turnover threshold or catered-supper remarks) is opinion rather than established fact
Some questions are only appropriate for certain company types, such as startups or private companies, as the README itself notes
